claims.text: The decoupled model will reduce lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction error by approximately 30–50% relative to traditional Debye-based estimates.
The model will independently capture the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity.
Below approximately 200 K, heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by phonon conduction.
Electron scattering is minimal below approximately 200 K in HfNbTaTiZr.
Above approximately 300 K, adding the separately modeled electronic contribution will produce total-conductivity predictions aligned with experiment.
The specimens are fully dense HfNbTaTiZr alloys produced by spark plasma sintering of gas-atomized powders.
The specimen set includes low-oxygen material and material deliberately doped to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Measured grain-size distributions, grain-boundary character, and defect and oxygen maps can be used to adjust DFT-derived scattering rates.
DFT-derived atomic-level properties can provide baseline inputs to separate Boltzmann transport models for phonons and electrons.
Microstructural corrections will produce more realistic phonon mean free paths.
Grain boundaries, defects, and oxygen-related microstructure will not significantly affect electronic transport.
The independently modeled phonon and electronic contributions can be summed to reproduce total observed thermal conductivity.
Earlier methods conflate lattice and electronic heat transport.
The 30–50% error reduction applies specifically to lattice-conductivity estimates over 50–200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits a crossover from low-temperature phonon-dominated transport to mixed conduction at higher temperatures.
Existing analytical and DFT models rely on idealized, defect-free bulk calculations.
Existing models cannot fully capture microstructural and impurity effects in real HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
The model is applicable only over 50–1200 K to SPS specimens made from gas-atomized powder with controlled oxygen content.

contradictions.description: The query states that experiments below 200 K indicate comparable lattice and electronic contributions, whereas the hypothesis predicts phonon-dominated transport with minimal electronic involvement in that range.

The mechanism assumes that microstructural corrections do not significantly affect electronic transport, while the uncertainty field acknowledges potentially important cross-effects between defects and electronic transport.
